## The debate

In 2006 Muhammad Yunus and the Grameen Bank he founded shared the Nobel Peace Prize. The committee praised their efforts to “create economic and social development from below” and linked lasting peace to large groups of people finding ways out of poverty.

Then came the randomized evaluations. In 2015 six were published together, covering six countries on four continents. Banerjee, Karlan and Zinman described a consistent pattern of modestly positive effects that were not transformative. A policy bulletin on seven evaluations stated plainly that microcredit does not have a transformative impact on poverty. Take-up was 13 to 31 percent in four of the countries, none of the studies found a significant rise in average household income, and none found widespread harm. Six found that households gained more freedom in how they earned, spent, invested and managed risk. Meager (2019) pooled seven experiments and concluded that the average effect on business activity and consumption is probably small and may be negligible.

The averages are not the whole story. Meager found that households already running a business gained more, though less predictably. In Hyderabad, India, researchers followed households for six years after microfinance arrived. Households that had run businesses before microfinance arrived ended up with about 35 percent more business assets and roughly double the revenue of similar households in control areas, while other households showed almost no effect. The authors argue that credit can help some talented, low-wealth entrepreneurs escape a poverty trap.

## Where Charitology stands

On the average effect, the debate has narrowed. Several rigorous studies agree that microcredit is not, on average, the transformation once hoped for. What remains open is partly empirical and partly about values. Whether gains for a minority justify a program for many, and how much flexibility is worth next to income, are value questions Charitology leaves to the giver. The history also bears on [the Story Bias](/diagnosis/story-bias/). Microcredit won worldwide recognition in 2006, and the main set of randomized results was published together in 2015. Charitology treats that gap as a feature of the system, not a failing of the people involved.
